Muslim World. The vast territories, diverse peoples, and civilizations united by Islamic faith and culture span from the seventh century onward, stretching from Spain to Central Asia to India. This civilization produced extraordinary advances in mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and philosophy while resisting European Crusades and sustaining complex trade networks. The Muslim world was never monolithic but rather a collection of competing sultanates, caliphates, and kingdoms navigating internal politics, theological disputes, and external pressures. It originated with the Prophet Muhammad's revelation in the seventh century and rapidly expanded through military conquest and conversion across three continents within a century. The Muslim world divided into numerous regional powers and dynasties rather than a single unified political entity. The Abbasid, Umayyad, Ottoman, and other caliphates each dominated different periods and regions. Centers of learning at Baghdad, Damascus, Cairo, and Córdoba preserved and advanced Greek and Roman knowledge while making original contributions to algebra, astronomy, optics, and medicine. The Muslim world resisted and ultimately defeated the Crusades launched from Christian Europe. Military leaders like Saladin recovered Jerusalem and established the limits of Christian military expansion. Throughout this period, Muslim territories connected continents through the Silk Road trade networks, exchanging spices, textiles, precious metals, and intellectual innovations with China, India, and Europe. However, internal division by sectarian differences between Sunni and Shia, ethnic rivalries, and competing dynastic claims prevented unified response to external threats until the Ottoman rise consolidated much of the Muslim world under a single power.
